### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
Over the next decades tensions remained high and the increased contact between Somali sailors and Ottomancorsairs worried the Portuguese who sent a punitive expedition under João de Sepúlveda, where he bombarded Mogadishu and captured Turkish vessels, compelling its ruler to sign a peace deal with the Portuguese. Barawa would also sign peace with the Portuguese after being sacked.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Sep%C3%BAlveda,_1542-53) The Ottoman-Somali cooperation against the Portuguese on the Indian Ocean reached a high point in the 1580s when Ajuran clients of the coastal cities began to cooperate with the Arabs and Swahilis under Portuguese rule and sent an envoy to the Turkish corsair Mir Ali Bey for a joint expedition against the Portuguese. He agreed and was joined by a Somali fleet in order to attack the Portuguese colonies in Southeast Africa.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch195025-54)
A 16th century map by Jan Huyghen[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-55)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
The Somali-Ottoman offensive managed to drive out the Portuguese from several important cities such as Pate, Mombasa and Kilwa. However, the Portuguese governor sent envoys to Portuguese India requesting a large Portuguese fleet. This request was answered and it reversed the previous offensive of the Muslims into one of defense. The Portuguese armada managed to re-take most of the lost cities and began punishing their leaders, but they refrained from attacking Mogadishu, securing the city's autonomy in the Indian Ocean.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-57) The Ottoman Empire would remain an economic partner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Shapes-12) Throughout the 16th and 17th centuries the Ajurans successively defied Portuguese hegemony on the Indian Ocean by employing a new coinage which followed the Ottoman pattern, thus proclaiming an attitude of economic independence in regard to the Portuguese.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-61)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
From the late 15th and up until the 17th centuries saw the arrival of Muslim families from Arabia, Persia, India and Spain to the Ajuran realm of territories, the majority of whom settled in the coastal provinces. Some migrated because of the instability in their respective regions, as was the case with the Hadhrami families from Yemen and Muslims from Spain fleeing the Inquisition.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-63) Others came to conduct business or for religious purposes. Due to their strong tradition in religious learning, the new Muslim communities also enjoyed high status among the Somali ruling elite and commoners.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-65)
The tomb of Sheikh Hussein
The most famous Somali scholar of Islam from the Ajuraan period is Sheikh Hussein, who was born in Merca, one of the power jurisdiction and cultural centers of the Ajuran Empire.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-66) He is credited with converting the Sidamo people living in the area of what is now the Bale Province, Ethiopia to Islam.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-67) He is also credited with establishing the Sultanate of Bale.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-69)
Despite the Bale Sultanate not being directly under Ajuran rule, the two kingdoms were deeply connected and Bale was heavily influenced by Ajuran. His tomb lies in the town of Sheikh Hussein in what is considered the most sacred place in the country for Ethiopian Muslims, in particular those of Oromo ethnic descent.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-71)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
In the mid-17th century, the Oromo people collectively began expanding from their homeland towards the southern Somali coast at a time when the Ajurans were at the height of their power.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982114-72) The Garen rulers conducted several military expeditions known as the _Gaal Madow_ _Wars,_ on the Oromo invaders, converting those that were captured to Islam.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-76)

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
[edit]
The Ajuran Empire slowly declined in power at the end of the 17th century. In this period the rulers of the empire abandoned Sharia, became oppressive and enacted heavy taxation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:4-9) The dethronement of the Muzaffar clients in Mogadishu and other coastal cities by the Abgaalimam who then established the Hiraab Imamate taking residence in Mogadishu was a significant setback,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewis198837-77) and the defeat of the Silcis vassals by a former Ajuran general in the interior of the state, Ibrahim Adeer, who established the Gobroon dynasty.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) By the early 1700s there was effectively no trace of Ajuran left in Banaadir.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:3-25)
Taxation and the practice of primae noctis were the main catalysts for the revolts against Ajuran rulers.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-80) The loss of port cities and fertile farms meant that much needed sources of revenue were lost to the rebels.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) Somali maritime enterprise significantly declined after the collapse of the Ajuran Empire. However, other principalities such as the Isaaq Sultanate, Warsangali Sultanate, Majeerteen Sultanate, and the Sultanate of Hobyo in a way ensured its continuity.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-81)

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
The city of Merca was a prominent administrative center of the Ajurans
The Ajuran nobility used many of the typical Somali aristocratic and court titles, with the Garen rulers styled Imam.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-82) These leaders were the empire's highest authority, and counted multiple Sultans, Emirs, and Kings as clients or vassals. The Garen rulers also had seasonal palaces in Mareeg, Qelafo and Merca, important cities in the Empire were Mogadishu and Barawa. The state religion was Islam, and thus law was based on Sharia.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-85)
1.   Imam – Head of State[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-86)  
2.   Emir – Commander of the armed forces and navy  
3.   [Na'ibs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Na'ib "Na'ib") – Viceroys[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-87)  
4.   Wazirs – Tax and revenue collectors  
5.   Qadis – Chief Judges

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
Through their control of the region's wells, the Garen rulers effectively held a monopoly over their nomadic subjects as they were the only hydraulic empire in Africa during their reign. Large wells made out of limestone were constructed throughout the state, which attracted Somali and Oromo nomads with their livestock.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Siedlak-88) The centralized regulations of the wells made it easier for the nomads to settle disputes by taking their queries to government officials who would act as mediators. Long distance caravan trade, a long-time practice in the Horn of Africa, continued unchanged in Ajuran times. Today, numerous ruined and abandoned towns throughout the interior of Somalia and the Horn of Africa are evidence of a once-booming inland trade network dating from the medieval period.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982149-89)
The Jubba River
With the centralized supervision of the Ajuran, farms in Afgooye, Kismayo and other areas in the Jubba and Shabelle valleys increased their productivity. A system of irrigation ditches known locally as _Kelliyo_ fed directly from the Shebelle and Jubba rivers into the plantations where sorghum, maize, beans, grain and cotton were grown during the _gu_ (Spring in Somali) and _xagaa_ (Summer in Somali) seasons of the Somali calendar. This irrigation system was supported by numerous dikes and dams. To determine the average size of a farm, a land measurement system was also invented with _moos_, _taraab_ and _guldeed_ being the terms used.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-90)
Mogadishan currency
The State collected tribute from the farmers in the form of harvested products like durra, sorghum and bun, and from the nomads, cattle, camels and goats. The collecting of tribute was done by a wazir. Luxury goods imported from foreign lands were also presented as gifts to the Garen rulers by the coastal sultans of the state.

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
A political device that was implemented by the Garen rulers in their realm was a form of _ius primae noctis_,[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-91) which enabled them to create marriages that enforced their hegemonic rule over all the important groups of the empire. The rulers would also claim a large portion of the bride's wealth, which at the time was 100 camels.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Siedlak-88)
For trade, the Ajuran Empire minted its own Ajuran currency.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Stgi-92) It also utilized the Mogadishan currency originally minted by the Sultanate of Mogadishu, which later became incorporated into the Ajuran Empire.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56) Mogadishan coins have been found as far away as present-day United Arab Emirates in the Middle East.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Ncaaroth-93)

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
The Ajuran State had a standing army with which the governors ruled and protected their subjects. The bulk of the army consisted of recruited soldiers who did not have any loyalties to the traditional Somali clan system, thereby making them more reliable.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-94)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli198290-95)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-96) The soldiers were recruited from the inter-riverine area; other recruits came from the surrounding nomadic region. Arab, Persian and Turkish mercenaries were at times employed as well.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982104-97)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-98)
Almnara Somalia defensive tower
In the early period, the army's weapons consisted of traditional Somali weapons such as swords, daggers, spears, battle axes, and bows. The Empire received assistance from the Ottoman Empire, and with the import of firearms through the Muzzaffar port of Mogadishu, the army began acquiring muskets and cannons.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-99)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-100)

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
The Ottomans would also remain a key ally during the Ajuran-Portuguese wars. Horses used for military purposes were raised in the interior, and numerous stone fortifications were erected to provide shelter for the army in the coastal districts.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli198292-101) In each province, the soldiers were under the supervision of a military commander known as an Emir.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli198290-95) The coastal areas and the lucrative Indian Ocean trade was protected by a navy.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch195025-54)

## Urban and maritime centers
[edit]
Ruins of Mareeg, capital of the Ajuran Empire, photographed by Neville Chittick in 1975.
The urban centers of Merca, Mogadishu, Barawa, and their respective ports became profitable trade outlets for commodities originating from the interior of the state.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-102) The farming communities of the hinterland brought their products to the coastal cities, where they were sold to local merchants who maintained foreign commerce with ships sailing to and from Arabia, India, Venice, Persia, Egypt, Portugal, and as far as China.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-103)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-104)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-106)
The walled city of Mogadishu on the 16th century Miller Atlas.

## Urban and maritime centers
Vasco da Gama, who passed by Mogadishu in the 15th century[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-107) noted that it was a large city with houses of four or five storeys high and big palaces in its centre and many mosques with cylindrical minarets.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-108)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-109) In the 16th century, Duarte Barbosa noted that many ships from the Kingdom of Cambaya sailed to Mogadishu with cloths and spices for which they in return received gold, wax and ivory.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-110)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-111) Barbosa also highlighted the abundance of meat, wheat, barley, horses, and fruit on the coastal markets, which generated enormous wealth for the merchants.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-112)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-113)
Citadel ruins of Gondershe

## Urban and maritime centers
Mogadishu, the center of a thriving weaving industry known as _toob benadir_ (specialized for the markets in Egypt and Syria),[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-114) together with Merca and Barawa also served as transit stops for Swahili merchants from Mombasa and Malindi and for the gold trade from Kilwa.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-115) There were Jewish merchants from the Hormuz who brought their Indian textile and fruits to the Somali coast in exchange for grain and wood.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-116)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-117)
Trading relations were established with Malacca in the 15th century,[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-118) with cloth, ambergris and porcelain being the main commodities of the trade.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-119) In addition, giraffes, zebras and incense were exported to the Ming Empire of China.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-120)Hindu merchants from Surat and Southeast African merchants from Pate seeking to bypass both the Portuguese blockade and Omani interference used the ports of Merca and Barawa (which were out of the two powers' jurisdiction) to conduct their trade in safety.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-121)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
Over the next decades tensions remained high and the increased contact between Somali sailors and Ottomancorsairs worried the Portuguese who sent a punitive expedition under João de Sepúlveda, where he bombarded Mogadishu and captured Turkish vessels, compelling its ruler to sign a peace deal with the Portuguese. Barawa would also sign peace with the Portuguese after being sacked.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Sep%C3%BAlveda,_1542-53) The Ottoman-Somali cooperation against the Portuguese on the Indian Ocean reached a high point in the 1580s when Ajuran clients of the coastal cities began to cooperate with the Arabs and Swahilis under Portuguese rule and sent an envoy to the Turkish corsair Mir Ali Bey for a joint expedition against the Portuguese. He agreed and was joined by a Somali fleet in order to attack the Portuguese colonies in Southeast Africa.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch195025-54)
A 16th century map by Jan Huyghen[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-55)
texts.10:
### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
The Somali-Ottoman offensive managed to drive out the Portuguese from several important cities such as Pate, Mombasa and Kilwa. However, the Portuguese governor sent envoys to Portuguese India requesting a large Portuguese fleet. This request was answered and it reversed the previous offensive of the Muslims into one of defense. The Portuguese armada managed to re-take most of the lost cities and began punishing their leaders, but they refrained from attacking Mogadishu, securing the city's autonomy in the Indian Ocean.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-57) The Ottoman Empire would remain an economic partner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Shapes-12) Throughout the 16th and 17th centuries the Ajurans successively defied Portuguese hegemony on the Indian Ocean by employing a new coinage which followed the Ottoman pattern, thus proclaiming an attitude of economic independence in regard to the Portuguese.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-61)
texts.11:
### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
From the late 15th and up until the 17th centuries saw the arrival of Muslim families from Arabia, Persia, India and Spain to the Ajuran realm of territories, the majority of whom settled in the coastal provinces. Some migrated because of the instability in their respective regions, as was the case with the Hadhrami families from Yemen and Muslims from Spain fleeing the Inquisition.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-63) Others came to conduct business or for religious purposes. Due to their strong tradition in religious learning, the new Muslim communities also enjoyed high status among the Somali ruling elite and commoners.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-65)
The tomb of Sheikh Hussein
The most famous Somali scholar of Islam from the Ajuraan period is Sheikh Hussein, who was born in Merca, one of the power jurisdiction and cultural centers of the Ajuran Empire.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-66) He is credited with converting the Sidamo people living in the area of what is now the Bale Province, Ethiopia to Islam.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-67) He is also credited with establishing the Sultanate of Bale.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-69)
Despite the Bale Sultanate not being directly under Ajuran rule, the two kingdoms were deeply connected and Bale was heavily influenced by Ajuran. His tomb lies in the town of Sheikh Hussein in what is considered the most sacred place in the country for Ethiopian Muslims, in particular those of Oromo ethnic descent.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-71)
texts.12:
### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
In the mid-17th century, the Oromo people collectively began expanding from their homeland towards the southern Somali coast at a time when the Ajurans were at the height of their power.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982114-72) The Garen rulers conducted several military expeditions known as the _Gaal Madow_ _Wars,_ on the Oromo invaders, converting those that were captured to Islam.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-76)
texts.13:
### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
[edit]
The Ajuran Empire slowly declined in power at the end of the 17th century. In this period the rulers of the empire abandoned Sharia, became oppressive and enacted heavy taxation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:4-9) The dethronement of the Muzaffar clients in Mogadishu and other coastal cities by the Abgaalimam who then established the Hiraab Imamate taking residence in Mogadishu was a significant setback,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewis198837-77) and the defeat of the Silcis vassals by a former Ajuran general in the interior of the state, Ibrahim Adeer, who established the Gobroon dynasty.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) By the early 1700s there was effectively no trace of Ajuran left in Banaadir.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:3-25)
Taxation and the practice of primae noctis were the main catalysts for the revolts against Ajuran rulers.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-80) The loss of port cities and fertile farms meant that much needed sources of revenue were lost to the rebels.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) Somali maritime enterprise significantly declined after the collapse of the Ajuran Empire. However, other principalities such as the Isaaq Sultanate, Warsangali Sultanate, Majeerteen Sultanate, and the Sultanate of Hobyo in a way ensured its continuity.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-81)
texts.14:
### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
The city of Merca was a prominent administrative center of the Ajurans
The Ajuran nobility used many of the typical Somali aristocratic and court titles, with the Garen rulers styled Imam.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-82) These leaders were the empire's highest authority, and counted multiple Sultans, Emirs, and Kings as clients or vassals. The Garen rulers also had seasonal palaces in Mareeg, Qelafo and Merca, important cities in the Empire were Mogadishu and Barawa. The state religion was Islam, and thus law was based on Sharia.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-85)
1.   Imam – Head of State[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-86)  
2.   Emir – Commander of the armed forces and navy  
3.   [Na'ibs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Na'ib "Na'ib") – Viceroys[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-87)  
4.   Wazirs – Tax and revenue collectors  
5.   Qadis – Chief Judges
texts.15:
### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
Through their control of the region's wells, the Garen rulers effectively held a monopoly over their nomadic subjects as they were the only hydraulic empire in Africa during their reign. Large wells made out of limestone were constructed throughout the state, which attracted Somali and Oromo nomads with their livestock.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Siedlak-88) The centralized regulations of the wells made it easier for the nomads to settle disputes by taking their queries to government officials who would act as mediators. Long distance caravan trade, a long-time practice in the Horn of Africa, continued unchanged in Ajuran times. Today, numerous ruined and abandoned towns throughout the interior of Somalia and the Horn of Africa are evidence of a once-booming inland trade network dating from the medieval period.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982149-89)
The Jubba River
With the centralized supervision of the Ajuran, farms in Afgooye, Kismayo and other areas in the Jubba and Shabelle valleys increased their productivity. A system of irrigation ditches known locally as _Kelliyo_ fed directly from the Shebelle and Jubba rivers into the plantations where sorghum, maize, beans, grain and cotton were grown during the _gu_ (Spring in Somali) and _xagaa_ (Summer in Somali) seasons of the Somali calendar. This irrigation system was supported by numerous dikes and dams. To determine the average size of a farm, a land measurement system was also invented with _moos_, _taraab_ and _guldeed_ being the terms used.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-90)
Mogadishan currency
The State collected tribute from the farmers in the form of harvested products like durra, sorghum and bun, and from the nomads, cattle, camels and goats. The collecting of tribute was done by a wazir. Luxury goods imported from foreign lands were also presented as gifts to the Garen rulers by the coastal sultans of the state.
texts.16:
### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
A political device that was implemented by the Garen rulers in their realm was a form of _ius primae noctis_,[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-91) which enabled them to create marriages that enforced their hegemonic rule over all the important groups of the empire. The rulers would also claim a large portion of the bride's wealth, which at the time was 100 camels.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Siedlak-88)
For trade, the Ajuran Empire minted its own Ajuran currency.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Stgi-92) It also utilized the Mogadishan currency originally minted by the Sultanate of Mogadishu, which later became incorporated into the Ajuran Empire.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56) Mogadishan coins have been found as far away as present-day United Arab Emirates in the Middle East.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Ncaaroth-93)
texts.17:
### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
The Ajuran State had a standing army with which the governors ruled and protected their subjects. The bulk of the army consisted of recruited soldiers who did not have any loyalties to the traditional Somali clan system, thereby making them more reliable.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-94)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli198290-95)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-96) The soldiers were recruited from the inter-riverine area; other recruits came from the surrounding nomadic region. Arab, Persian and Turkish mercenaries were at times employed as well.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982104-97)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-98)
Almnara Somalia defensive tower
In the early period, the army's weapons consisted of traditional Somali weapons such as swords, daggers, spears, battle axes, and bows. The Empire received assistance from the Ottoman Empire, and with the import of firearms through the Muzzaffar port of Mogadishu, the army began acquiring muskets and cannons.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-99)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-100)
texts.18:
### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
The Ottomans would also remain a key ally during the Ajuran-Portuguese wars. Horses used for military purposes were raised in the interior, and numerous stone fortifications were erected to provide shelter for the army in the coastal districts.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli198292-101) In each province, the soldiers were under the supervision of a military commander known as an Emir.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli198290-95) The coastal areas and the lucrative Indian Ocean trade was protected by a navy.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch195025-54)
texts.19:
## Urban and maritime centers
[edit]
Ruins of Mareeg, capital of the Ajuran Empire, photographed by Neville Chittick in 1975.
The urban centers of Merca, Mogadishu, Barawa, and their respective ports became profitable trade outlets for commodities originating from the interior of the state.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-102) The farming communities of the hinterland brought their products to the coastal cities, where they were sold to local merchants who maintained foreign commerce with ships sailing to and from Arabia, India, Venice, Persia, Egypt, Portugal, and as far as China.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-103)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-104)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-106)
The walled city of Mogadishu on the 16th century Miller Atlas.
texts.20:
## Urban and maritime centers
Vasco da Gama, who passed by Mogadishu in the 15th century[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-107) noted that it was a large city with houses of four or five storeys high and big palaces in its centre and many mosques with cylindrical minarets.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-108)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-109) In the 16th century, Duarte Barbosa noted that many ships from the Kingdom of Cambaya sailed to Mogadishu with cloths and spices for which they in return received gold, wax and ivory.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-110)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-111) Barbosa also highlighted the abundance of meat, wheat, barley, horses, and fruit on the coastal markets, which generated enormous wealth for the merchants.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-112)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-113)
Citadel ruins of Gondershe
texts.21:
## Urban and maritime centers
Mogadishu, the center of a thriving weaving industry known as _toob benadir_ (specialized for the markets in Egypt and Syria),[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-114) together with Merca and Barawa also served as transit stops for Swahili merchants from Mombasa and Malindi and for the gold trade from Kilwa.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-115) There were Jewish merchants from the Hormuz who brought their Indian textile and fruits to the Somali coast in exchange for grain and wood.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-116)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-117)
Trading relations were established with Malacca in the 15th century,[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-118) with cloth, ambergris and porcelain being the main commodities of the trade.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-119) In addition, giraffes, zebras and incense were exported to the Ming Empire of China.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-120)Hindu merchants from Surat and Southeast African merchants from Pate seeking to bypass both the Portuguese blockade and Omani interference used the ports of Merca and Barawa (which were out of the two powers' jurisdiction) to conduct their trade in safety.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-121)
